"As a rule, freely permitted", with conditions Advocate General Szpunar's opinion in Like Company v. Google (C- 250/25), the first generative AI case before the EU's top court, says training can fall under the TDM exception if developers: 1 Use lawfully accessible sources: no pirate sites, no getting around paywalls or bot blocks. 2 Respect opt-outs: a machine-readable reservation, such as robots.txt, takes the work out. 3 Prevent memorisation: show steps taken so the model doesn't reproduce specific works. But: a chatbot fetching and reusing news articles in real time may still infringe press publishers' rights. The opinion is non-binding; the Court's judgment is pending. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 03 / 08

Fair use will be decided without a trial 4 Sept OpenAI, Microsoft, the news plaintiffs and the authors file cross- motions for summary judgment in In re OpenAI Copyright Infringement Litigation (SDNY). Late Oct Dozens of amicus briefs on both sides, from Hollywood unions and publishers to libraries and the EFF. The US government backs fair use. 6 Nov Judge Sidney Stein allows 56 amicus briefs. His ruling will be the first fair use decision involving OpenAI and the news cases. Earlier US rulings on AI training came from two California judges. A New York ruling on news content could shape licensing worldwide. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 05 / 08

India shouldn't leave this to one interim order. Stretching "private use, including research" to cover commercial AI training is a fragile base for a whole industry. A clear statutory rule, like the EU's opt-out model with transparency and anti-memorisation duties, would serve creators and developers better than case- by-case guesswork. Adv.
